src: site, modelled on FA24 Exam 2, Q6B
stem:
1,2-Dibromoethane reacts with the dianion of benzene-1,2-diol. Two of the products have the formulas {{C8H8O2}} and {{C10H12Br2O2}}. Draw each.
[[rxn:BrCCBr + [O-]c1ccccc1[O-]>>"C8H8O2" + "C10H12Br2O2"]]
model:
{{C8H8O2}}: one dianion and one dibromide, both bromines gone. Two {{SN2}} reactions, the second one intramolecular, close a six-membered ring.

[[mol:C1COc2ccccc2O1]]

{{C10H12Br2O2}}: one dianion and two dibromides. Each oxygen attacks a different molecule of dibromide, and each dibromide keeps one bromine.

[[mol:BrCCOc1ccccc1OCCBr]]

rubric.h: C8H8O2: the ring with O-CH2-CH2-O fused to the benzene ring
C10H12Br2O2: the open chain with a BrCH2CH2O group on each ring oxygen
Says each product comes from two SN2 reactions, the ring from an intramolecular second step
Shows the count of pieces or checks the formulas

steps.h: The dibromide is {{C2H4Br2}}: a {{C2H4}} chain with a bromine on each end. The dianion is {{C6H4O2}} with two negative charges.

ask.a: One C-Br bond becomes one C-O bond. One {{Br-}} leaves and one negative charge on oxygen is used up.

steps.h: {{C8H8O2}} has no bromine and two oxygens. {{C6H4O2}} plus {{C2H4}} is {{C8H8O2}}: one of each piece, and both ends of the dibromide have reacted.

ask.q: One dianion, one dibromide, no bromine left. What shape must it be?
ask.a: A ring: the second oxygen attacks the other end of the same two-carbon chain.

steps.h: O, C, C, O and the two ring carbons that carry the oxygens: a six-membered ring fused to the benzene ring.
{{C10H12Br2O2}} has two bromines and two oxygens. {{C6H4O2}} plus two {{C2H4Br}} is {{C10H12Br2O2}}: one dianion and two dibromides, each having lost one bromine.

ask.q: Where is the dianion in this product, in the middle or at an end?
ask.a: In the middle. Each of its oxygens is bonded to a different {{CH2CH2Br}} chain.

steps.h: Phenoxide oxygens are good nucleophiles and weak bases (phenol {{pKa}} 10), and the carbons attacked are primary: {{SN2}}, not elimination.
Count every atom of each structure against its formula. Every {{CH2}} of the dibromide is still a {{CH2}}.

solution.answer: C8H8O2 is the six-membered cyclic diether fused to the benzene ring. C10H12Br2O2 is the benzene ring with two OCH2CH2Br groups on neighbouring carbons.
solution.rule: No halogen left and one of each piece: a ring. Two halogens left: the dinucleophile is in the middle.

stem:
1,4-Dibromobutane and sodium sulfide ({{Na2S}}) give two products, {{C4H8S}} and {{C8H16Br2S}}. Draw each, and write the mechanism that leads to the first.
[[rxn:BrCCCCBr + [Na+].[Na+].[S-2]>>"C4H8S" + "C8H16Br2S"]]
model:
{{C4H8S}}: one sulfide and one dibromide. The sulfur bonds to both ends of the same chain: a five-membered ring.

[[mol:C1CCSC1]] [[mech:thiolane-sulfide-dibromobutane]]

{{C8H16Br2S}}: one sulfide and two dibromides. After the first {{SN2}} the thiolate attacks a second molecule of dibromide instead of its own chain.

[[mol:BrCCCCSCCCCBr]]

rubric.h: C4H8S: the five-membered ring with one sulfur
C8H16Br2S: Br(CH2)4S(CH2)4Br
Mechanism to the ring: two SN2 steps with correct arrows and the thiolate intermediate
Counts the pieces or checks the formulas

steps.h: The dibromide is a {{C4H8}} chain with a bromine on each end. The nucleophile is one sulfur atom with two negative charges.

ask.q: How many carbons can one sulfide ion bond to?
ask.a: Two. It has two negative charges, so it can do {{SN2}} twice and end up neutral.

steps.h: {{C4H8S}}: one {{C4H8}} chain, one sulfur, no bromine. Both ends of one chain are on the same sulfur.

ask.a: Five atoms: the sulfur and four carbons.

steps.h: {{C8H16Br2S}}: two {{C4H8}} chains, one sulfur, two bromines. The sulfur is in the middle and each chain keeps its far bromine.
Sulfide attacks an end carbon and bromide leaves: a thiolate. The thiolate then attacks either the other end of its own chain (the ring) or a second dibromide (the open chain).

ask.q: Which reagent in excess favours the open chain?
ask.a: The dibromide: the thiolate then meets another dibromide molecule more often.

steps.h: No hydrogens gained or lost: eight in the ring, sixteen in the chain.

solution.answer: C4H8S is the five-membered cyclic sulfide (thiolane). C8H16Br2S is bis(4-bromobutyl) sulfide.
solution.rule: A nucleophile with two charges on one atom bonds to two carbons: the same chain gives a ring, two chains give a sulfide in the middle.

stem:
1,4-Dibromobutane is treated with two equivalents of NaCN in DMSO. The product is {{C6H8N2}}. Which structure is it?
[[rxn:BrCCCCBr + [Na+].[C-]#N>DMSO>"C6H8N2"]]

choices.why: Each cyanide replaces one bromine and brings its own carbon: four {{CH2}} groups plus two CN groups is {{C6H8N2}}.
This is what one equivalent gives: {{C5H8BrN}}. It still has a bromine and has only one nitrogen.
This counts the nitrile carbons as part of the four-carbon chain. It is {{C4H4N2}}: two carbons and four hydrogens short.
This has an elimination at one end: {{C5H7N}}. Cyanide with a primary halide substitutes, and the formula has two nitrogens.

steps.h: A {{C4H8}} chain with two bromines, and cyanide, CN, which attacks with its carbon.

ask.q: How many nitrogens are in the product, and what does that tell you?
ask.a: Two, so two cyanides are in it: both bromines have been replaced.

steps.h: {{C4H8}} plus two CN is {{C6H8N2}}. The formula matches a chain with a nitrile at each end.

ask.q: Why can there be no ring here?
ask.a: Each cyanide has one charge and makes one bond. Once bonded it cannot attack again.

steps.h: The chain between the two nitrile carbons is still four {{CH2}} groups. The product has six carbons, not four.

ask.q: How many hydrogens should the product have?
ask.a: Eight: the four {{CH2}} groups are unchanged.

steps.h: A bromine left, too few carbons, or a C=C: each wrong choice fails the count.

solution.rule: Two equivalents of a singly charged nucleophile: both halogens replaced, open chain. Cyanide adds a carbon each time.

stem:
1,3-Dibromopropane reacts with two equivalents of sodium methanethiolate. The product is {{C5H12S2}}. Which structure is it?
[[rxn:BrCCCBr + C[S-].[Na+]>>"C5H12S2"]]

choices.why: Each thiolate replaces one bromine: {{C3H6}} plus two {{CH3S}} groups is {{C5H12S2}}.
Only one substitution: {{C4H9BrS}}. The formula has two sulfurs and no bromine.
A ring would need one sulfur to bond to both ends, but each sulfur already carries a {{CH3}} and has only one charge. This is {{C3H6S}}.
Elimination at one end gives {{C4H8S}}. Thiolates are weak bases and excellent nucleophiles: they substitute.

steps.h: {{C3H6}} with two bromines; {{CH3S-}} with one charge.
Two sulfurs, no bromine: two thiolates, both ends substituted.
{{C3H6}} plus two {{CH3S}} is {{C5H12S2}}.

solution.rule: A nucleophile with one charge makes one bond: two equivalents give an open chain.

stem:
1,4-Dibromobutane and sodium azide ({{NaN3}}) in DMF give {{C4H8N6}} when two equivalents of azide are used, and mostly {{C4H8BrN3}} when one equivalent is used. Draw both products.
[[mol:BrCCCCBr]]
model:
{{C4H8N6}}: six nitrogens are two azide groups. Both bromines are replaced.

[[mol:[N-]=[N+]=NCCCCN=[N+]=[N-]]]

{{C4H8BrN3}}: three nitrogens are one azide group. One bromine is replaced and one is left.

[[mol:[N-]=[N+]=NCCCCBr]]

rubric.h: C4H8N6: an azide group on each end of the four-carbon chain
C4H8BrN3: an azide on one end, bromine on the other
Reasoning: nitrogens divided by three gives the number of azides; each SN2 replaces one bromine

steps.h: {{C4H8}} with two bromines; azide, {{N3-}}, a good nucleophile (8,000 on the lecture scale) with one charge.
Six nitrogens: two azides. Three nitrogens: one azide.
None left in the first product; one left in the second.
Eight in both: the four {{CH2}} groups are unchanged.

solution.rule: The number of equivalents decides how many halogens are replaced.

stem:
1,5-Dibromopentane and sodium sulfide give this ring. What is its molecular formula?
[[rxn:BrCCCCCBr + [Na+].[Na+].[S-2]>>C1CCSCC1]]

choices.why: Five {{CH2}} groups and one sulfur. Both bromines have left as bromide.
This adds sulfur without removing the bromines. Each C-S bond is made by pushing a bromide out.
Two hydrogens too many: this is an open-chain compound. The ring has only {{CH2}} groups.
This is the other product, the open chain with two dibromide pieces on one sulfur.

steps.h: Five carbons and one sulfur.
Each carbon is a {{CH2}}: ten hydrogens. Sulfur carries none.
Two {{SN2}} reactions, two bromide ions lost.

solution.rule: Product formula = the pieces minus the leaving groups.

stem:
Dibromomethane reacts with propane-1,3-dithiolate. Two of the products are {{C4H8S2}} and {{C5H10Br2S2}}. Draw each.
[[rxn:BrCBr + [S-]CCC[S-]>>"C4H8S2" + "C5H10Br2S2"]]
model:
{{C4H8S2}}: one dithiolate and one {{CH2}}. Both sulfurs bond to the same carbon and close a six-membered ring.

[[mol:C1CSCSC1]]

{{C5H10Br2S2}}: one dithiolate and two dibromomethanes. Each sulfur attacks a different {{CH2Br2}}, which keeps one bromine.

[[mol:BrCSCCCSCBr]]

rubric.h: C4H8S2: six-membered ring with one CH2 between the two sulfurs (1,3-dithiane)
C5H10Br2S2: BrCH2S(CH2)3SCH2Br
Says both come from two SN2 reactions
Counts the pieces or checks the formulas

steps.h: Dibromomethane is one {{CH2}} with two bromines. The dithiolate is {{C3H6S2}}.
{{C3H6S2}} plus {{CH2}} is {{C4H8S2}}, no bromine: a ring. The single carbon sits between the two sulfurs: S, C, S, then three carbons, six atoms.
{{C3H6S2}} plus two {{CH2Br}} is {{C5H10Br2S2}}: the dithiolate in the middle, a {{CH2Br}} on each sulfur.
The exam's {{C4H8S2}} was a ring with two carbons between the sulfurs on each side. Same formula, different ring: here the pieces are one carbon and three carbons.

solution.rule: The formula gives the pieces; the pieces give the connections. Keep each piece intact.

stem:
1,5-Dibromopentane is warmed with excess methylamine (the extra amine removes the N-H protons). One product is {{C6H13N}}. Which structure is it?
[[rxn:BrCCCCCBr + CN>>"C6H13N"]]

choices.why: One nitrogen, no bromine: the same nitrogen has attacked both ends of the chain, losing a proton each time. Five {{CH2}} groups, N and {{CH3}}: {{C6H13N}}.
Two amines, one at each end: {{C7H18N2}}. The formula has only one nitrogen.
This stops after one substitution: {{C6H14BrN}}. The formula has no bromine.
The formula fits, but the methyl has moved from nitrogen to carbon. No bond to the methyl carbon is made or broken in an {{SN2}} at the chain ends.

steps.h: A {{C5H10}} chain with two bromines; methylamine, {{CH3NH2}}, a neutral nucleophile with two N-H bonds.
One nitrogen, no bromine: one amine has reacted with both ends.
{{C5H10}} plus {{CH3N}} is {{C6H13N}}: the amine has lost both of its N-H hydrogens, one after each {{SN2}}.
The {{CH3}} stays on nitrogen. Ring: N plus five carbons, six atoms.

solution.rule: An amine with two N-H bonds can act as a dinucleophile on one atom.

stem:
1,4-Dibromobutane reacts with sodium acetylide. With two equivalents the product is {{C8H10}}; with one equivalent it is mostly {{C6H9Br}}. Draw both.
[[rxn:BrCCCCBr + [Na+].[C-]#C>>"C8H10"]]
model:
{{C8H10}}: both bromines replaced. Each acetylide attacks with its charged carbon and adds two carbons.

[[mol:C#CCCCCC#C]]

{{C6H9Br}}: one bromine replaced.

[[mol:C#CCCCCBr]]

rubric.h: C8H10: a terminal alkyne at each end of the four-carbon chain
C6H9Br: an alkyne at one end, bromine at the other
Says acetylide attacks through carbon (SN2 at a primary carbon), adding two carbons each time
Checks the formulas

steps.h: {{C4H8}} with two bromines; acetylide, {{HC≡C-}}, which is {{C2H}} with one charge on carbon. It is a top nucleophile in the lecture table (126,000).
{{C4H8}} plus two {{C2H}} is {{C8H10}}: both ends substituted.
{{C4H8Br}} plus one {{C2H}} is {{C6H9Br}}: one end substituted.

steps.t: Draw the new bonds in the right place
steps.h: The new C-C bond is to the carbon that carried the charge. The other alkyne carbon keeps its hydrogen.

solution.rule: Carbon nucleophiles lengthen the chain: count their carbons in the formula.

src: site, a variation on FA24 Exam 2, Q6B
stem:
On the exam, 1,2-diiodoethane and ethane-1,2-dithiolate gave {{C4H8S2}} and {{C6H12S2I2}}. This time a large excess of the dithiolate is used, and dilute acid is added at the end. The products are {{C4H8S2}} and {{C6H14S4}}. Draw both, and explain why the open-chain product has changed.
[[rxn:ICCI + [S-]CC[S-]>;then H3O+>"C4H8S2" + "C6H14S4"]]
model:
{{C4H8S2}} is the same ring as before: one of each piece, two {{SN2}} reactions.

[[mol:C1CSCCS1]]

{{C6H14S4}}: four sulfurs are two dithiolates, and there is no iodine, so both ends of one diiodide have reacted. With dithiolate in excess, each end of the diiodide meets a different dithiolate. The two outer sulfurs are left as thiolates, and the acid turns them into S-H.

[[mol:SCCSCCSCCS]]

rubric.h: C4H8S2: 1,4-dithiane
C6H14S4: HSCH2CH2SCH2CH2SCH2CH2SH
Explanation: with excess dithiolate the diiodide is in the middle and thiolate ends are left over, protonated by the acid
Counts the pieces or checks the formulas

steps.h: The diiodide is {{C2H4}} with two iodines. The dithiolate is {{C2H4S2}} with two charges.

steps.t: Count sulfurs and halogens in the new formula
steps.h: Four sulfurs: two dithiolates. No iodine: one diiodide with both ends substituted. Carbons: three {{C2H4}} units, six.
Three {{C2H4}} units give twelve hydrogens. The other two come from the acid: the two sulfurs that never found a carbon are protonated to S-H.
Excess diiodide puts a diiodide on each end of a dithiolate (the exam). Excess dithiolate puts a dithiolate on each end of a diiodide (here).

solution.answer: C4H8S2 is 1,4-dithiane. C6H14S4 is the open chain HS-CH2CH2-S-CH2CH2-S-CH2CH2-SH.
solution.rule: The reagent in excess ends up on the outside of the open-chain product.

stem:
1,3-Dibromopropane and ethane-1,2-dithiolate give the ring {{C5H10S2}}, and also a little of a compound {{C10H20S4}}. Which structure is {{C10H20S4}}?
[[rxn:BrCCCBr + [S-]CC[S-]>>"C5H10S2" + "C10H20S4"]]

choices.why: Two dithiolates and two dibromides joined alternately into one large ring: every three-carbon chain sits between two sulfurs, every sulfur is bonded to two carbons, and no bromine is left.
These are two separate molecules of the small ring, each {{C5H10S2}}. A molecular formula describes one molecule.
The atom count fits, but this has an S-S bond and a five-carbon chain. {{SN2}} at carbon only makes C-S bonds here, and the pieces stay intact.
An open chain of two dithiolates and one dibromide is {{C7H16S4}}, and it would need acid to put H on the end sulfurs.

steps.h: The dibromide gives {{C3H6}}; the dithiolate is {{C2H4S2}}. One of each is {{C5H10S2}}, the seven-membered ring.
{{C10H20S4}} is exactly twice {{C5H10S2}}: two dibromides and two dithiolates in one molecule, with no bromine and no S-H.
No ends left over means a ring. Join the pieces alternately: dithiolate, {{C3H6}}, dithiolate, {{C3H6}}, and back to the start.

steps.t: Test each choice against the pieces
steps.h: Every sulfur must be bonded to one two-carbon chain and one three-carbon chain. Only the large ring passes.

solution.answer: The large ring made of two dithiolates and two three-carbon chains, joined alternately
solution.rule: A formula that is double the small ring is one molecule built from two of each piece.
